passage: It rained so hard that recess was indoors, and Manjula ma'am paired everyone up for drawing. Nilesh got Bittu. Nilesh groaned. Last week he had seen Bittu peep at Rani's paper during the spelling test, and since then everything about Bittu seemed wrong. Bittu drew a tiger with stripes that curled like real fur. "It's ugly," Nilesh said. Bittu offered him the good orange crayon. He's only being nice so I won't tell, Nilesh thought, and pushed it back. When ma'am held up the tiger for the class, everyone clapped. Nilesh didn't. "He probably traced it," he whispered. But there was nothing to trace from. Bittu had drawn it right there, next to him, in the rain.

qa.q: What did Bittu draw?
qa.a: A tiger with stripes that curled like real fur.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh call the tiger ugly?
qa.a: He felt suspicious and resentful of Bittu since seeing him peep in the test, so even the good drawing and the kind crayon seemed bad or fake.

qa.q: What could help Nilesh see Bittu more fairly?
qa.a: Keeping the cheating separate from everything else, and noticing what he actually saw today, like Bittu drawing the tiger right beside him.

qa.q: How might Bittu feel when Nilesh pushes the crayon back?
qa.a: Bittu may feel hurt and confused, since he was only trying to share.

grounding: A boy who saw a classmate cheat once now sees his drawing and his kindness as bad too.

passage: In the lane behind their Kolkata building, Anirban watched Tuhin nudge a carrom coin with his sleeve when he thought nobody was looking. From then on, Anirban was sure Tuhin was rotten through and through. When Tuhin scored in football the next evening, Anirban said it was a foul. When Tuhin shared his jhalmuri with the little kids, Anirban muttered that he was showing off. On Friday a birthday card came under their door: "Please come, Anirban! Tuhin." "I'm not going," he told his sister Arohi. "He's a cheat." Arohi raised an eyebrow. "He cheated at carrom once. Does that make his jhalmuri a cheat too?" Anirban frowned at the card, which had a drawing of two boys playing football.

qa.q: How did Tuhin cheat at carrom?
qa.a: He nudged a carrom coin with his sleeve when he thought nobody was looking.

qa.q: Why did Anirban think sharing jhalmuri was showing off?
qa.a: He felt distrustful of Tuhin after the carrom cheat, so even kind acts looked fake to him.

qa.q: What small step could Anirban take about the birthday card?
qa.a: Think about Tuhin's other actions on their own, like sharing with the little kids, and perhaps go to the party.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Anirban's view of Tuhin?
qa.a: Arohi thinks it is unfair, pointing out that one carrom cheat doesn't make everything Tuhin does bad.

grounding: After seeing a boy cheat once at carrom, a child decides his goals, his sharing and his friendliness are all bad.

passage:
"Vicky won the science prize? That's so unfair."
"Kamal, did you see his model?" asked Tanuja, stirring the dal.
"I didn't need to. He cut the corner in the sports-day race. He's a cheater."
"In the race, yes. What was the model?"
"Some water filter. With sand and stones. Probably copied."
"From where?"
"I don't know. Somewhere."
"Did it work?"
Kamal kicked the chair leg. "The water came out clean. Everyone saw."
"So the race was wrong, and the filter worked."
"But he's a cheater, Ma."
"He cheated once, in the race. Is that the same as copying a model?"
Kamal went quiet. "Also he carried my bag when I hurt my ankle," he said slowly. "I forgot that."

qa.q: What was Vicky's science model?
qa.a: A water filter with sand and stones.

qa.q: Why does Kamal assume Vicky copied the model?
qa.a: He feels bitter and distrustful after seeing Vicky cut the corner in the race, so everything Vicky does seems like cheating.

qa.q: How does Tanuja help Kamal think more fairly?
qa.a: She asks simple questions about the model itself, separating the race from the filter until Kamal remembers Vicky's kindness too.

qa.q: What might Vicky feel if he heard Kamal call his prize unfair?
qa.a: Vicky might feel hurt, since his filter really worked and he had helped Kamal when his ankle was hurt.

grounding: A boy who saw a classmate cheat in a race assumes his prize-winning model must be copied too.

passage:
Monday. In the first week of Class 9, Amandeep fell asleep in the last period after a night of helping at his father's dhaba. Jahnavi ma'am woke him in front of everyone. "Our lazy Amandeep," she said, and the class laughed. The name stuck.
Wednesday. Amandeep handed in the history project two days early, with maps he had drawn by hand. Ma'am took it without a word. That afternoon he forgot his geometry box, and she said loudly, "Of course. Lazy Amandeep." He stared at his desk, face burning.
Friday. The projects came back. His had a B and one line: "Neat, but late effort as usual." It had not been late. Amandeep turned the page over so nobody could see, and didn't raise his hand once all day, even when he knew the answer.

qa.q: What did Amandeep draw by hand for the history project?
qa.a: Maps.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when his project came back?
qa.a: He felt hurt and defeated, because his early, careful work was called late, as if the label mattered more than what he actually did.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to see Amandeep fairly?
qa.a: Check the facts, like the early submission, look at each piece of work on its own, and ask why he was so tired that first week.

qa.q: What might change if Jahnavi ma'am had asked why Amandeep was sleepy?
qa.a: She would learn he had been helping at his father's dhaba, and the lazy label might never have started.

grounding: Over a week, a boy labelled lazy by a teacher finds his early, careful work ignored while every small slip is pointed out.

passage: Sahil, you think your teacher has decided you're a troublemaker and nothing will change it? Let your Sumit chacha tell you what happened to me at fourteen. In Class 8 I threw a paper ball once, just once, and it hit Mr Bhalla. From that day I was "the naughty one." If anyone talked, he looked at me. When I won the inter-house quiz, he said, "Even naughty boys get lucky." When I forgot my tie, it was "typical." I stopped trying. Why bother? Then in Class 10 a new teacher, Mrs Dsouza, arrived. She didn't know the label. She read my essay out loud and said, "Who wrote this? It's excellent." The whole class turned to look at me. I'll never forget how strange it felt to be seen.

qa.q: What did Mr Bhalla say when young Sumit won the quiz?
qa.a: "Even naughty boys get lucky."

qa.q: Why did young Sumit stop trying in Mr Bhalla's class?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and unfairly judged, because his wins were called luck and every small slip was called typical.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sumit's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: A new teacher who didn't know the label praised his essay; being judged on his actual work let him feel seen again.

qa.q: How might Mrs Dsouza have felt reading the essay aloud?
qa.a: She was probably pleased and curious, simply enjoying good writing with no label in the way.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, as a teenager labelled naughty, his wins were called luck and his slips typical, until a new teacher saw his work.

passage: The board practical was starting in ten minutes when the lab's water tap burst, spraying the benches. Bhupen, nearest, dived under the sink and shut the valve with his bare hands, soaking his shirt. When Mr Gogoi rushed in, he saw only Bhupen, dripping, next to the broken tap. "Bhupen again! Always some trouble with you." Bhupen opened his mouth, but the invigilator was already calling roll numbers, and there was no time. All through the exam he sat in a wet shirt, hands shaking, getting the titration wrong twice. Afterwards Ira, who had seen everything, went straight to Mr Gogoi. "Sir, he stopped the water. We'd have lost the whole lab." Mr Gogoi paused, then looked at Bhupen's wet shirt for a long moment.

qa.q: How did Bhupen stop the water?
qa.a: He dived under the sink and shut the valve with his bare hands.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel sitting the exam in a wet shirt?
qa.a: He was upset and shaken, hands trembling, after being blamed for the burst tap he had actually stopped.

qa.q: What could Mr Gogoi have done differently when he rushed in?
qa.a: Ask what happened before blaming anyone, instead of letting the trouble label decide what he saw.

qa.q: How might Ira feel after telling Mr Gogoi the truth?
qa.a: Ira may feel nervous but relieved, glad to have stood up for Bhupen.

grounding: Under exam pressure, a boy with a troublemaker label is blamed for the burst tap he actually stopped.

passage: The week the market research report was due, Lars sent his section to the group two hours after the deadline. Mei, who was coordinating the group at their Stockholm university, fixed the formatting at midnight and decided that was that. For the next project she gave everyone tasks except Lars. "Just review, if you want," she wrote to him. When he offered to run the survey, she said she'd already done it. When he spotted an error in her chart, she thought, typical, nitpicking because he can't do the real work. Only at the final presentation did the professor mention that Lars had topped the statistics exam. Mei stared at him. She had never once asked what he was good at.

qa.q: How late was Lars's section?
qa.a: Two hours after the deadline.

qa.q: Why did Mei dismiss Lars's correction of her chart?
qa.a: She felt irritated and already sure he was useless, so even a helpful catch looked like nitpicking.

qa.q: What could Mei try after a single late submission?
qa.a: Ask what happened, and give Lars a real task to see his work, rather than letting one delay define him.

qa.q: How might Lars feel being told to just review?
qa.a: He might feel sidelined and frustrated, especially after offering to run the survey and spotting a real error.

grounding: After one late submission, a student decides a groupmate is useless and stops giving him tasks, missing his real strengths.

passage: In the college robotics lab, the club had three weeks to build a line-following robot. In week one, Ramesh submitted the wiring diagram a day late. Samir, the team lead, sighed loudly in front of everyone. After that, he gave Ramesh nothing but cable-cutting. When Ramesh suggested a better sensor layout, Samir waved him off. "Let's stick to what works." The robot kept veering off the line. At 11 p.m. on the last night, with the lab assistant waiting to lock up, Samir was out of ideas. Ramesh quietly moved two sensors, the same layout he had suggested in week two. The robot followed the line perfectly. Samir looked at the sensors, then at Ramesh. "Why was your diagram late, that first week?" "My grandmother was in hospital," Ramesh said.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do on the last night?
qa.a: He moved two sensors, the same layout he had suggested in week two.

qa.q: Why did Samir wave off Ramesh's sensor idea?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and a bit dismissive of Ramesh after one late diagram, so the idea didn't seem worth hearing.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Samir treated Ramesh, and what could fix it?
qa.a: He let one late diagram define Ramesh; asking why it was late and judging each idea on its merits would fix it.

qa.q: What was the project like for Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh was stuck cutting cables while his grandmother was ill and his good idea was ignored, which must have felt lonely and unfair.

grounding: A team lead decides a member is useless after one late diagram and ignores his idea until the last night.

passage:
Hi Swati,
About the case competition: I think we should take Dev off the finance section. He sent his part of the practice round a day late, and honestly, if he can't manage one deadline, I don't trust him with the numbers. I've moved his section to myself and given him the slides to format. I know he said something about his laptop crashing, but everyone has excuses.
Also, I saw his comment on our group doc suggesting a different valuation method. I didn't reply. He's probably just trying to look busy after the late submission.
Let's finalise the team plan tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Dev say had happened?
qa.a: Something about his laptop crashing.

qa.q: Why doesn't Asif trust Dev with the numbers?
qa.a: Asif feels irritated and sure that one late submission shows Dev is unreliable, so even his useful suggestion looks like an act.

qa.q: What would you advise Asif before taking Dev off finance?
qa.a: Check the laptop story, read Dev's valuation suggestion properly, and judge him on more than one late part.

qa.q: How might Dev feel if he learns he has been moved to formatting slides?
qa.a: Dev would likely feel hurt and shut out, having explained the crash and offered a real idea that got no reply.

grounding: A student writes to a co-lead that a groupmate should lose his tasks after one late submission, dismissing his explanation and ideas.

passage:
Dear Karthik,
I want to be honest about something before your probation review on Friday. Two weeks ago you sent the client the wrong invoice, and I was angry. For a few days after that, I noticed I was reading everything you did through that mistake. A short email looked careless. A question looked like you didn't know the basics.
So this week I made myself look at your whole record: three months of client notes, the backlog you cleared in March, the feedback from the Hyderabad team. I also checked the invoice system, and it turns out the template had been changed that morning without anyone telling you.
My recommendation is to confirm you. Let's work out an invoice checklist together.
Ayesha

qa.q: What had happened to the invoice template that morning?
qa.a: It had been changed without anyone telling Karthik.

qa.q: What did Ayesha notice about the feelings after the invoice mistake?
qa.a: Ayesha noticed being angry and reading everything through that one mistake, so even a short email felt careless.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do before deciding, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Reviewed the whole three-month record and checked the context of the invoice, so one error didn't decide Karthik's future.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Karthik might feel relieved and respected, and perhaps surprised at how honest Ayesha is about the anger.

grounding: A young lead writes that one error had coloured the lead's view, and that the full record and context were reviewed before deciding.

passage: Kamal, the thing I'm proudest of this month is something I almost did wrong. You know Ravi, the new waiter at our café? On Saturday, the busiest night, he dropped a full tray in front of a table of twelve. I was furious. And for the next week, every time I looked at him I saw that tray. He was two minutes late; I thought, careless. He forgot one order; I thought, of course. I was about to cut his shifts. Then I stopped and asked myself, Jahnavi, is this about Ravi or about Saturday? So I pulled his three months of shift notes. Almost no complaints, and two thank-you cards from customers. And that Saturday? He'd been covering two sections because someone called in sick. I kept his shifts.

qa.q: How many customer thank-you cards did Ravi have?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel after the dropped tray?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt furious, and for a week that anger made every small slip by Ravi look careless.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do before cutting Ravi's shifts?
qa.a: Asked whether the anger was about Ravi or about Saturday, then pulled his three months of notes and checked the context of that night.

qa.q: What was that Saturday night really like for Ravi?
qa.a: Ravi was covering two sections because someone called in sick, so he was probably rushed and stressed when he dropped the tray.

grounding: A young café manager notices one mistake colouring the manager's view of a waiter and checks his full record and context before deciding.

passage: I've sat across from Uma in the site office for a year, so I saw how the Omkar business went. Omkar, the new site engineer, signed off a delivery of the wrong grade of steel in his second week. Uma was livid; I heard her on the phone. For days after that she double-checked everything he touched. But one evening I saw her doing something different. She had his whole file open: his inspection reports, the three safety issues he had caught in his first week, the call logs from the supplier. She even rang the supplier herself. It turned out the delivery note had the right grade printed on it; the wrong bars had been loaded by mistake. Next morning she told him, "I was judging you by one day. That wasn't fair." I can't say what she felt, but her shoulders looked lighter.

qa.q: What did Omkar sign off in his second week?
qa.a: A delivery of the wrong grade of steel.

qa.q: What might Uma's lighter shoulders suggest?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and lighter after looking at the full record and admitting she had been unfair.

qa.q: What did Uma do that made her judgment fairer?
qa.a: She reviewed Omkar's whole file and called the supplier to learn the context before deciding.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when Uma says she was judging him by one day?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and respected, after days of having everything he touched double-checked.

grounding: A colleague describes a young lead who noticed one error colouring her view and reviewed the engineer's full record and context.

passage:
Monday
Today in the lunch line Wasim bumped me so hard my dal spilled on my shoe. He didn't even say sorry. He is SO mean. I told Rinku he does it on purpose because he thinks he's the boss of Class 4.
After lunch the bell rang and everyone ran for the stairs. I was squashed between big kids and I stepped on a little girl's foot. She cried. I said "sorry, it was crowded!" and ran. It WAS crowded.
Now I'm lying in bed thinking. The lunch line was crowded too. Wasim was holding his tray with both hands.
Maybe he's not mean. Maybe it was just the line.
Ramesh

qa.q: What happened to Ramesh's dal?
qa.a: It spilled on Ramesh's shoe.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh think Wasim bumped on purpose?
qa.a: Ramesh felt angry and embarrassed about the spilled dal, so it seemed Wasim must be mean, without thinking about the crowded line.

qa.q: What question could Ramesh ask the next time someone bumps into him?
qa.a: Was it crowded or rushed, the way the stairs were when Ramesh stepped on the girl's foot?

qa.q: How might the little girl on the stairs see Ramesh?
qa.a: She might think Ramesh was mean or careless, the same way Ramesh judged Wasim.

grounding: A child's diary shows blaming a classmate's character for a bump while excusing their own bump as the crowd's fault.

passage: The morning bus to the taluk school was so packed that boys hung from the door rail. When it stopped at Chetan's village, Minakshi from the next lane shoved past him, and his tiffin box fell in the dust. "Rude!" Chetan shouted after her. "She thinks she owns the bus." He brushed off the box, fuming, and squeezed in last. At the next stop the bus braked suddenly, and Chetan fell against an old man with a basket of brinjals. "Sorry, Dadaji! The driver braked," he said, cheeks red. The old man nodded. "It's a crowded bus, beta." Chetan looked down the aisle at Minakshi, squashed between two women with bundles, her own bag held over her head.

qa.q: What happened to Chetan's tiffin box?
qa.a: It fell in the dust.

qa.q: Why did Chetan decide Minakshi was rude?
qa.a: He felt angry and embarrassed when his tiffin fell, so her character, not the packed bus, seemed to be to blame.

qa.q: What could Chetan remember the next time he is pushed on the bus?
qa.a: That the bus is crowded for everyone, just as it was when he fell against the old man, so a push may not mean someone is rude.

qa.q: How does the old man see Chetan bumping into him?
qa.a: The old man sees it as the crowded bus, not a rude boy, and calmly accepts the apology.

grounding: A boy calls a girl rude for pushing past on a packed bus, then excuses his own bump as the driver's braking.

passage: On the school skating day at the outdoor rink in Oslo, Xin was gliding slowly near the edge when Lars crashed into him and they both went down. "You did that on purpose!" Xin shouted. "You're always showing off." Lars, red-faced, said the ice was bumpy there, but Xin didn't listen. He told his friends Lars was a bully. Twenty minutes later, Xin hit the same bumpy patch, lost his balance and knocked over a smaller girl. "Sorry! The ice is terrible here!" he said, helping her up. On the bus home, rubbing his elbow, Xin remembered Lars saying almost exactly those words. He looked across at Lars, who was quietly picking ice out of his gloves.

qa.q: What did Lars say about the ice?
qa.a: That it was bumpy there.

qa.q: Why did Xin call Lars a bully?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry after falling, so it seemed Lars must be showing off, even though Lars mentioned the bumpy ice.

qa.q: What could Xin do after noticing his own fall?
qa.a: Give Lars the same fair reading he gave himself, and perhaps apologise for calling him a bully.

qa.q: How might Lars feel being called a bully after an accident?
qa.a: Lars probably felt embarrassed and unfairly judged, since he explained about the ice and wasn't believed.

grounding: A boy blames another child's character for a crash on the ice, then blames the ice when he causes the same kind of fall.

passage:
Vaibhav,
I'm writing this because you clearly don't read messages. I sent you eleven texts yesterday about the dance audition. Eleven. You saw them, I'm sure, and you didn't reply to one. On my big day. I thought we were friends, but I guess you only care when you need notes before exams. Chitra said you were probably busy with cricket. Busy for a whole day? No. You just don't care about anyone except yourself, and I'm done pretending you do.
Don't bother replying now.
Kavitha
PS. Your mum called my mum this morning, something about your Nani and the hospital. I didn't listen properly. Doesn't change anything.

qa.q: How many texts did Kavitha send about the audition?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why is Kavitha so sure Vaibhav doesn't care?
qa.a: Kavitha feels hurt and angry on the big day, so the silence seems to prove Vaibhav is selfish, and the news about Nani and the hospital barely registers.

qa.q: What would you advise Kavitha before sending this?
qa.a: Wait, and ask what happened, especially after the call about Nani and the hospital; there may be a family crisis behind the silence.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav's day have been like?
qa.a: Vaibhav may have been at the hospital with Nani, worried and away from the phone, with no room to think about texts.

grounding: A teenager writes off a friend as uncaring for not replying, while barely noticing news of a family crisis.

passage: Ritu, I'm telling you, Farah is the worst. We planned to go to the book fair at four, right? I waited at the gate for forty minutes. Forty! I messaged her six times, called her twice. Nothing. Not even a sorry. This is just who she is. She did the same thing in Class 7 when she forgot my birthday. She thinks her time matters more than everyone else's. What? No, her phone was fine yesterday. Why would it suddenly... okay, it's old, fine, it dies sometimes. But she could have borrowed someone's. Unless she wasn't near anyone. Or... no. Look, Preeti knows people, and Farah just doesn't care. Why are you shaking your head?

qa.q: How long did Preeti wait at the gate?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why does Preeti decide Farah doesn't care?
qa.a: Preeti feels hurt and annoyed after waiting, so the silence feels like proof of Farah's character, and the old phone that dies seems like an excuse.

qa.q: What could Preeti try before deciding what Farah is like?
qa.a: Wait until Farah can explain, and think about ordinary reasons first, like a dead phone or being stuck somewhere.

qa.q: Why might Ritu be shaking her head?
qa.a: Ritu probably thinks Preeti is being unfair, blaming Farah's character before knowing what happened.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend that another friend's no-show proves she doesn't care, brushing past the chance of a dead phone.

passage:
Thursday. Leela sent Kishore the photos from the science exhibition: their project, their prize. Blue ticks. No reply. By night she had typed, "wow ok thanks for caring," and sent it.
Friday. Kishore wasn't in school. Leela told the group, "He's probably sulking because I got the stage for the prize." Someone laughed. She felt clever, and a little sick.
Sunday. Kishore's cousin posted in the class group: Kishore's father had been in a road accident on Thursday evening; he was stable now, and Kishore had been at the hospital for three days. Leela read it standing in the kitchen. She scrolled up to her own message, "thanks for caring," and her hand went cold. Then she typed, slowly, "I'm so sorry. I didn't know. Can I bring you food?"

qa.q: Where had Kishore been for three days?
qa.a: At the hospital, after his father's road accident.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she read the cousin's post?
qa.a: She felt shocked and ashamed, her hand going cold as she saw how wrong her message had been.

qa.q: What did Leela do right on Sunday, and what could she have done on Thursday?
qa.a: She apologised and offered food; on Thursday she could have asked if Kishore was okay instead of assuming he didn't care.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel seeing "thanks for caring" among his messages?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and too tired to explain, having spent three days at the hospital with his father.

grounding: Over a few days, a teenager decides a friend's silence means he doesn't care, then learns of a family emergency.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
Karthik slept through our group meeting AGAIN. Third time. He sat in the library corner with his head on the table while Swara and I did the literature review. Swara nudged him and he mumbled sorry. Honestly, some people just don't want to work. I told Swara we should mark his contribution as zero in the peer review.
Came back late tonight from the canteen and saw him at the bus stop with a call-centre ID card and a headset round his neck, catching the 10:40 night bus. He didn't see me.

Yash

qa.q: What was Karthik wearing at the bus stop?
qa.a: A call-centre ID card and a headset round his neck.

qa.q: What is Yash feeling at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Yash feels uneasy and a little guilty, realising Karthik might be working nights and was never asked why he was tired.

passage: At the government college in Mandya, the soil-testing assignment was due Monday, and Raju had missed three of their four morning lab slots. Jagdish complained loudly in the canteen. "He's lazy. Comes at eleven, yawning, as if we're his servants." He was halfway to the lecturer's cabin to report him when Usha caught his arm. "You know Raju works the night shift at the sugar mill in crushing season? It ends at six. He cycles eight kilometres to get here." Jagdish stopped. "He never told anyone." "You never asked," Usha said. "His father's been ill." Jagdish looked down the corridor at Raju, asleep sitting up on the bench outside the lab, a soil sample bag still in his hand.

qa.q: How far does Raju cycle to college?
qa.a: Eight kilometres.

qa.q: Why was Jagdish so sure Raju was lazy?
qa.a: He felt annoyed at doing Raju's share, and without knowing about the night shift, laziness seemed the only explanation.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do instead of reporting Raju?
qa.a: Talk to Raju and plan the assignment so Raju takes tasks that fit his hours, perhaps with the lecturer's help.

qa.q: What is it like for Raju during crushing season?
qa.a: Raju works nights at the mill, cycles eight kilometres and falls asleep on the bench, probably exhausted and worried about his father.

grounding: A student is about to report a groupmate as lazy until he learns the groupmate works night shifts at a mill.

passage:
"Vishal, got a minute?" Sarika pulled a chair to his desk. "The last three reports had the client's name spelled wrong."
Vishal rubbed his eyes. "I know. I'm sorry."
"I'm not here to scold. I'm curious. What's been going on?"
He hesitated. "We moved my mother in with us last month. She needs help at night. I've been sleeping maybe four hours."
"That sounds really hard."
"But also," he said, "I've never been great at proofreading. Even before."
"Okay. So maybe both things are true." Sarika nodded slowly. "For the tired part, could you do reports in the morning instead of late evening? And for the habit, want to try reading them aloud before sending? It works for me."
Vishal let out a long breath. "I thought you were going to call me careless."
"I nearly did," she admitted. "Then I wondered what I didn't know."

qa.q: How many hours has Vishal been sleeping?
qa.a: Maybe four hours.

qa.q: Why did Sarika start by asking what was going on?
qa.a: She felt curious rather than angry, wondering what she didn't know before deciding he was careless.

qa.q: Why is Sarika's two-part plan wise?
qa.a: It deals with both causes: moving reports to the morning for the tiredness, and reading aloud for the proofreading habit.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel after the conversation?
qa.a: Vishal feels relieved, letting out a long breath, because he expected to be called careless and was asked about his life instead.

grounding: A young colleague asks what is happening for a teammate before calling him careless, and accepts that both a situation and a habit are true.

passage: Last spring Joseph started arriving late to our 9 a.m. stand-ups, three or four times a week. My first thought was the obvious one: he doesn't care any more. I actually drafted a message to our manager. But I've learned, the hard way, that I'm quick to decide things about people, so I deleted it and asked Joseph for tea instead. "Everything okay? You've been missing the mornings." He looked embarrassed. His building's water came only between eight and nine, and he was filling buckets for his elderly neighbours. "But honestly," he added, "I've always been bad with mornings." Both were true. We moved the stand-up to 9:30, and he set two alarms. He hasn't missed one since. The team calls me "Samir the detective" now. I'd rather be Samir who asks.

qa.q: When did Joseph's building get water?
qa.a: Only between eight and nine.

qa.q: Why did Samir delete the drafted message?
qa.a: Samir felt wary of judging people too quickly, and was curious enough to ask Joseph before deciding he didn't care.

qa.q: How did the team handle both reasons for Joseph's lateness?
qa.a: They moved the stand-up to 9:30 for the water timing, and Joseph set two alarms for his own morning habit.

qa.q: How did Joseph seem to feel when Samir asked?
qa.a: Joseph seemed embarrassed but honest, sharing both the water problem and his trouble with mornings.

grounding: A young colleague recalls asking a late teammate what was happening instead of judging him, and finding both a situation and a habit.

passage:
Team supervisor's note, customer support, 3 October
Eshaan's call ratings have dropped this month, and two customers complained that he sounded distracted. I had half decided to put him on a warning. Before I did, Sangeeta, who trained him, asked to speak to him first. She told me afterwards what she had asked: not "Why are you careless?" but "What's been happening for you lately?" Eshaan told her his younger brother had exams and the family had only one laptop, so he had been taking calls on a borrowed phone with a poor headset. He also admitted he had never been good at taking notes during calls. Sangeeta arranged an office headset for him and set up a simple note template. I have held off the warning and will review his ratings in a month.

qa.q: What was Eshaan taking calls on?
qa.a: A borrowed phone with a poor headset.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta's question suggest about her attitude?
qa.a: She was curious and caring rather than quick to blame, wanting to understand what was happening for Eshaan before deciding.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta address both the situation and the habit?
qa.a: She arranged an office headset for the borrowed-phone problem and a note template for his weak note-taking.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel after the conversation with Sangeeta?
qa.a: Eshaan probably felt relieved and supported, since he was asked about his life instead of warned.

grounding: A supervisor records a young trainer asking what was happening for a struggling colleague before calling him careless, and finding two causes.

passage: The colony match was cut to five overs because dark clouds were rolling in, and Varun's team had to bat fast. He hit two fours and a six, and they won with one ball left before the rain came down. "Did you see my shots?" he said to his sister Aparna, dripping on the doormat. "Pure talent. I read the bowler perfectly." Next Sunday, same five overs, same clouds. Varun was out first ball, bowled. "The bat's handle is loose," he announced, "and the umpire moved when the bowler ran in. Distracting." Aparna, who had watched from the balcony both times, handed him a towel. "Last week the bat was fine and the umpire was great?" Varun opened his mouth, then took the towel without answering.

qa.q: How many overs was the colony match cut to?
qa.a: Five overs.

qa.q: Why did Varun blame the bat and the umpire the second Sunday?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at being out first ball, so blaming the bat and umpire protected his pride, while the win had felt like pure talent.

qa.q: What could Varun ask himself after both matches?
qa.a: What part was his skill and what part was luck or conditions, asked the same way for the win and the loss.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Varun's two explanations?
qa.a: Aparna sees they don't match, noticing he credited himself for the win and blamed the bat and umpire for the loss.

grounding: A boy credits his own talent for a win and blames the bat and the umpire for a loss under the same conditions.

passage: On Sunday afternoon in their Jaipur flat, Mridul beat his sister Bhavna at ludo twice in a row. "I'm a genius at strategy," he announced, dancing round the sofa. "You have to plan every move." Bhavna rolled her eyes and set up the board again. In the third game, her tokens raced home while Mridul's stayed stuck at the start. He lost. "This dice is broken," he said, shaking it. "It only gives me ones." "Same dice as the first two games," said Bhavna. "Those were different. That was skill." Their grandfather looked up from his newspaper. "So the dice only breaks when you lose, Mridul?" Mridul folded his arms, glanced at the dice, then at Dadaji, and grinned a little sheepishly.

qa.q: How many times in a row did Mridul beat Bhavna?
qa.a: Twice in a row.

qa.q: Why did Mridul blame the dice in the third game?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and embarrassed at losing, so a broken dice was easier to believe than bad luck, while his wins had felt like genius.

qa.q: What could Mridul notice from Dadaji's question?
qa.a: That luck played a part in all three games, so the wins weren't only skill and the loss wasn't only the dice.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel hearing Mridul call his wins genius?
qa.a: Bhavna is probably amused and a bit annoyed, since the same dice decided every game.

grounding: A boy calls his board-game wins genius and blames the dice when he loses.

passage:
"We won the first round because of my smash, Ma. Nobody can return it."
"And the semi-final?"
"The shuttle was feathery. And the referee called my serve out when it was totally in."
Rukmini set down two glasses of lassi. "So the first match was you, and the second match was the shuttle and the referee?"
"Yes. Obviously."
"Was the shuttle feathery in the first match?"
"...Same box."
"Was the referee the same?"
"Mm."
"Nilesh, if the other boy said he lost the first round because of the shuttle, what would you say?"
"That he's making excuses."
Rukmini raised her eyebrows and sipped her lassi.
Nilesh groaned. "Okay, okay. Maybe my backhand was bad in the semi."
"Want to practise it tomorrow?"
"...Fine."

qa.q: What did Nilesh say about the shuttle in the semi-final?
qa.a: The shuttle was feathery.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh credit his smash for the win but blame the shuttle for the loss?
qa.a: He feels proud of winning and embarrassed about losing, so owning the win and blaming the shuttle protects how he sees himself.

qa.q: How did Rukmini help Nilesh see it differently?
qa.a: She asked whether the shuttle and referee were the same both times, then turned it round to the other boy's excuses, so he admitted his weak backhand.

qa.q: How might the boy who beat Nilesh feel if he heard about the feathery shuttle?
qa.a: He might feel his win was being dismissed, since he played with the same shuttle and referee.

grounding: A boy credits his smash for a win and blames the shuttle and referee for a loss, until his mother's questions help him see it.

passage: When the mock results came out at their school in Dublin, Liam got 91 in maths and 48 in history. "Maths? I'm just naturally good at it," he told Bilal at the bus stop. "Didn't even revise much." "And history?" "Ms Doyle marks unfairly. And the essay question was ridiculous. Nobody could have answered it." Bilal checked his own sheet. "I got 74 in history. Same question." Liam shrugged. "You got lucky with it." "I revised that chapter for two weeks," Bilal said. "You told me it was boring." Liam looked at the bus timetable very hard. The bus was late. He said it was the driver's fault.

qa.q: What did Bilal score in history?
Why does Liam blame Ms Doyle for his history mark?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed about the low mark, so blaming the teacher and the question protects his image as naturally clever.

qa.q: What could Liam learn from Bilal's history result?
qa.a: That two weeks of revision, not luck, made the difference, so he could revise that chapter instead of blaming the paper.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel when Liam calls his mark lucky?
qa.a: Bilal may feel annoyed and dismissed, since he revised for two weeks while Liam called the chapter boring.

grounding: A teenage boy credits his high maths mark to natural talent and blames the teacher and the question for his low history mark.

passage: At the coaching centre in Kota, results went up on the notice board every Monday. Week three, Jagdish was rank 4. "Natural talent," he told the canteen, loud enough for everyone to hear. "Some people just get physics." Week four, he was rank 63. He stood in front of the board with his arms folded. "Paper was set wrong. Half the questions were out of syllabus. And the invigilator kept walking around, so I couldn't focus." Payal, from his batch, was standing beside him. "Rank 4 last week, same invigilator." "That was different." "And the out-of-syllabus questions were from chapter nine, which we did on Saturday. You skipped Saturday." Jagdish's ears went red. "Whatever," he said, and walked off. But on Wednesday he was the first to ask for the chapter nine notes.

qa.q: What rank did Jagdish get in week four?
qa.a: Rank 63.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish blame the paper and the invigilator in week four?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and defensive about the drop, so blaming outside causes protected his picture of himself as naturally talented.

qa.q: What did Jagdish finally do that helps him learn?
qa.a: He asked for the chapter nine notes, dealing with the real gap instead of blaming the paper.

qa.q: How does Payal see Jagdish's excuses?
qa.a: Payal sees through them, pointing out the same invigilator last week and the Saturday class he skipped.

grounding: A teenage boy credits a high rank to natural talent and blames the paper and invigilator when his rank falls.

passage:
Hey Sahil,
Board pre-results are out. English: 94. I think I just have a gift for writing; I barely opened the textbook. Mrs Nair even read my essay out in class.
Chemistry: 52. Honestly, that paper was a disaster. The questions were framed to confuse us, the lab viva was on a day I had a headache, and Mr Pillai obviously doesn't like me. Even my answer sheet had a smudge on page three. Nothing I could have done.
Anyway, how did yours go? You said you were worried about chemistry too.
Chaitanya
PS. Mummy asked if I'd finished the organic revision plan. I told her it doesn't matter, the paper was unfair anyway.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya score in chemistry?
Why does Chaitanya say nothing could have been done about chemistry?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels embarrassed about the low mark and protects a gifted self-image by blaming the paper, the teacher and a headache.

qa.q: What would help Chaitanya learn from the chemistry result?
qa.a: Looking at the unfinished organic revision plan and the actual mistakes, and asking what was in Chaitanya's control, just as the English success is claimed.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about Chaitanya's answer about revision?
qa.a: Mummy might feel worried and a little frustrated, since the unfinished plan is waved away by blaming the paper.

grounding: A teenager writes that a high English mark shows a gift and a low chemistry mark was the paper's and teacher's fault.
